progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m7-c07 (complete and incomplete combustion equations; the data values −726, −1367, −2021, −2676 kJ/mol; soot means too little oxygen; a simple can catches about half; the spirit-burner set-up plate). chem-m6-c03 (q = mcΔT, c = 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹, ΔH = −q ÷ n, kJ, "keep the digits; round at the end"; recommended prerequisite, change 10). chem-m6-p02 (the error chain source to ΔT to q to ΔH; not every error pushes the same way; extrapolating a cooling line; validity, reliability and accuracy for a calorimetry practical; recommended prerequisite). chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability, accuracy, variables and risk assessment in plain words). chem-m7-c05 (alcohol names). Year 11: molar mass, n = m ÷ M; significant figures. Not assumed: spirit burner, draught shield (given a plain meaning), GHS hazard codes.

teaching.task: Your spirit burner will catch only about half the energy of each alcohol. So how do you measure the enthalpy of combustion of several alcohols, compare them reliably anyway, and explain where the rest of the energy goes?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a simple can catches about half the energy; the practical must compare alcohols reliably anyway (1); (2) heat must get into the water through the base, so a metal can sits close above the flame; a shield and a lid cut heat carried away by air (2); (3) the cap stops evaporation being counted as fuel burnt; the highest reading is the rise (3); (4) hotter water loses heat faster, so the same rise keeps the heat lost from the water similar for every alcohol (4); (5) the water's mass sets q; the fuel's mass lost sets n; ΔH = −q ÷ n per mole of fuel (5); (6) the values grow more negative with chain length, but each is about half (6); (7) trials agree, and the gaps between alcohols dwarf the spread, so the order is reliable (7); (8) heat to the can, clamp and air, incomplete combustion and soot make q too small; evaporation makes n too big; most errors make ΔH less negative, but not every one (8); (9) the flame loses heat for minutes, so extrapolation helps little; stop the loss at its source (9); (10) each improvement fixes a named cause; repeats fix reliability only (10); (11) one variable changed with losses similar makes the comparison valid; measuring only the water's heat makes each value less valid as an absolute measure (11); (12) the hazards and their controls (12); memory aid (13); attempts and brief feedback (14 to 17); decision rule and handoff (18); key notes (19).
teaching.conversationalApproach: the last video's methanol caught only about half the energy, which is normal for a spirit burner, so the practical asks how to measure the enthalpy of combustion of several alcohols, compare them reliably anyway and explain where the rest goes. Each part of the set-up is given its reason (a metal can close above the flame, a draught shield and lid, a capped burner), the method weighs the burner and records the highest temperature, and the same 20 degree rise keeps the heat lost similar for every alcohol. The calculation is staged one line at a time: the water's mass goes into q, the fuel's mass lost gives n, and delta H is minus q over n. Three trials per alcohol agree within about two per cent and the gaps between alcohols dwarf the spread, so the ranking is reliable but not accurate; the error chain traces heat to the can, clamp and air, incomplete combustion and evaporation through q or n to delta H, extrapolation helps only a little because the flame loses heat for minutes, and each improvement fixes a named cause while repeats fix reliability only. Validity and the risk assessment follow. The memory aids are water in q, fuel in n, and shield, lid, close, cap. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In the last video, burning methanol under a can of water caught only about half the energy. That's normal for this practical. So how do you measure the enthalpy of combustion of several alcohols, compare them reliably anyway, and explain where the rest of the energy goes?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A spirit burner containing ethanol (M = 46.07 g mol⁻¹) is used to heat 200.0 g of water from 20.3 °C to 38.9 °C. The mass of the spirit burner decreases from 158.42 g to 157.36 g. The specific heat capacity of water is 4.18 J g⁻¹ °C⁻¹. Calculate the molar enthalpy of combustion of ethanol." New numbers (the scenes work methanol); every given is on the card. Answer −676 kJ/mol (3 s.f.), 49.4% of −1367. Crossed mistake: the fuel's mass in q (1.06 × 4.18 × 18.6 = 82.4 J, giving about −3.58 kJ/mol), the 2019 Q23 marker-reported mistake (`../research/question-types-chem-m7.md`). (A2) "A student burns methanol and then butan-1-ol in a spirit burner beneath an uncovered copper can, with no draught shield, heating the water by 20 °C each time. Her mean molar enthalpies of combustion are −310 kJ mol⁻¹ for methanol and −1050 kJ mol⁻¹ for butan-1-ol. The data values are −726 kJ mol⁻¹ and −2676 kJ mol⁻¹. Each was repeated three times. Explain why her values are less negative than the data values, and suggest one improvement that would reduce this difference." Tests the error chain and an improvement matched to its cause. Answer: heat lost to the air and can (no shield, no lid), so q too small, ΔH less negative; a draught shield and lid. Crossed mistake: "repeat more times" (repeats improve reliability, not accuracy).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct a practical investigation to measure and reliably compare the enthalpy of combustion for a range of alcohols" "describe the procedures required to safely handle and dispose of organic substances (ACSCH075)" (carried by the risk table, change 5 of the route review) this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the spirit-burner investigation; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches: the set-up (spirit burner, metal can of water clamped close above the flame, draught shield, lid, heatproof mat) and why each part is there; the method (measured water, burner weighed with its cap on before and after, starting and highest temperatures, the same temperature rise for each alcohol, capping just before that rise to put the flame out, reweighing straight away); the variables of a comparison (independent: the alcohol; dependent: the molar enthalpy from ΔT and mass lost; controlled: water mass, can, flame distance, shield, lid, temperature rise), and why the same rise keeps losses comparable; the molar calculation in three stages with "water in q, fuel in n"; a results table for methanol to butan-1-ol, means of three trials; why the comparison is reliable (trials agree, and the gaps between alcohols are far bigger than the spread); why the values are inaccurate (about half the data values), traced through the error chain (heat to the can, clamp and air; incomplete combustion and soot; evaporation from the wick); why extrapolation helps little here, unlike chem-m6-p02; improvements matched to their causes; validity for comparing against validity as an absolute measure; the risk assessment and disposal of the alcohols. Recalled, not re-taught: q = mcΔT and c (chem-m6-c03); the error chain, "not every error pushes the same way", extrapolation and the meanings of validity, reliability and accuracy (chem-m6-p02, chem-m5-p01); combustion equations, incomplete combustion, the data values and "about half" (chem-m7-c07). Not here: anomalous results and further calculation practice (chem-m7-g02); answer technique for practical questions (s07); the bomb calorimeter and its figures (site correction 11); percentage uncertainty arithmetic; the calorimeter's heat capacity as a calculation.

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key as chem-m6-p02 and chem-m7-c07: heat warm-orange arrows; the temperature and balance readouts amber digits; the four alcohols in fixed colours across table rows, graph points and chips (methanol teal, ethanol amber, propan-1-ol violet, butan-1-ol blue); data values grey; q boxes orange, n boxes blue in the error chain; soot charcoal; hazards terracotta, controls green. Board layout (three zones, constant, as chem-m6-p02): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the apparatus or the graph; the right third holds the current card (method step, working, table, error chain, risk table), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every label dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: `m6-measuring-cylinder-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: an empty clear glass measuring cylinder with a hexagonal base, faint unlabelled graduations; scene 3, coded fill to 200 mL and coded label); `m7-ethanol-fuel-bottle-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: an amber glass bottle with a glass stopper, pale liquid, no label; scene 12 as an alcohol stock bottle, with a coded label); `m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: clear safety glasses; risk table head, "always"); `m5x-waste-bottle-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: an amber jar with a black cap and a blank cream label; scene 12, coded label "Organic waste"); `m7-fume-cupboard-v1.png` (2000 × 2000: a white fume cupboard with its sash part open; scene 12, small, beside "refill away from flames", tagged "or a refilling station, per school"). Considered, not used: `c8-thermometer-hot-v1.png` (inspected: a free-standing glass thermometer; the set-up plates include their own thermometer, and a separate one could not be placed in the can reliably); `m6-analytical-balance-v1.png` (inspected: an analytical balance with a glass draft enclosure holding a small beaker; a spirit burner is weighed on a top-pan balance, and the enclosure would hide or misplace it); `m6-foam-cup-calorimeter-v1.png` and `p02-foam-cup-in-beaker-v1.png` (neutralisation; shown only as a small grey thumbnail in scene 9's p02 recall, tagged "neutralisation practical"); `m5x-bunsen-burner-v1.png` (a gas burner, not a spirit burner). New plates: four (see Assets). No human figures.
